questions.prompt: Why can chasing another person weaken your position in this chapter?
choices: Because it often means accepting their timing and field first
Because movement is always irrational
Because the chapter says direct action never works

explanation.gentle: Yes. The law treats pursuit as a possible concession because it often means adapting to the other side's structure first.
explanation.direct: Chasing is costly here because it can donate initiative before the visible contest has really started.
explanation.competitive: Right. The moment you run onto their board, you start paying the tax.

questions.prompt: What does movement onto another person's ground usually change?
choices: Only the physical distance between people
Tempo, initiative, and who adapts first
Nothing important if the goal is good enough

explanation.gentle: That is the chapter's point. Movement changes more than distance because it shifts control and timing.
explanation.direct: Approach matters because whoever crosses first often reveals more need and adapts sooner.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The first crossing is often the first concession.

questions.prompt: What is bait doing in this law when it works well?
choices: It guarantees deception without any cost
It proves that passivity is always stronger than action
It creates a reason for the other side to approach on your chosen terms

explanation.gentle: Yes. The bait functions as invitation or inducement that pulls movement toward your field.
explanation.direct: The mechanism is controlled approach. The other side crosses toward a structure you already arranged.
explanation.competitive: Correct. Their motion starts doing your work.

questions.prompt: Lila keeps chasing a slow client through repeated follow-up emails. What move best fits the chapter?
choices: Keep increasing the frequency so the client feels pressure
Create a clearer time-bound opening that makes the client return if the opportunity matters
Withdraw every option permanently so no one can say she chased

explanation.gentle: That fits the law. She shifts from pursuit to inducement without collapsing into total passivity.
explanation.direct: Option B preserves more initiative by changing who has to make the next movement. A is just harder chase, and C destroys the field entirely.
explanation.competitive: Right. She stops paying the tax and makes the client spend it if the deal is real.

questions.prompt: Owen's business fair table keeps getting ignored. What principle should guide the fix?
choices: Set up the table so passersby feel drawn to approach instead of chasing each one manually
Assume quality alone will eventually make people stop
Abandon the table and spend the whole event pursuing traffic in the hallway

explanation.gentle: Yes. The chapter values a better field that draws movement more than exhausting pursuit.
explanation.direct: He needs architecture that changes approach, not more donated movement from his side.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. The table should start pulling so he can stop sprinting.

questions.prompt: Sasha keeps sending messages into a tense silence. What is the sharper Chapter 8 question?
choices: How can she make the other person feel guilty faster
How can she create a clearer reopening point instead of donating more movement
How can she disappear forever so pursuit becomes impossible

explanation.gentle: That is the more strategic question. The chapter asks whether chasing is improving the field or only showing more need.
explanation.direct: Option B turns the problem into movement control. A is crude pressure, and C mistakes withdrawal for architecture.
explanation.competitive: Right. She has to rebuild the route, not just run it harder.

questions.prompt: Why can induced approach be stronger than blunt pursuit?
choices: Because it removes the need for any real objective
Because it guarantees the other side will not notice the tactic
Because it lets the other side spend effort and reveal interest first

explanation.gentle: Yes. Once the other side chooses motion, they have already started adapting to your field.
explanation.direct: Induced approach is stronger because movement itself becomes evidence of interest and a shift in tempo.
explanation.competitive: Correct. The crossing already makes them pay part of the tax.

questions.prompt: When does bait start failing under this law?
choices: When it is subtle enough that the other side barely notices the structure
When it becomes obvious, too costly, or exposes too much need
Only when the other side has already agreed with you verbally

explanation.gentle: That is the boundary. Bad bait reveals anxiety instead of control.
explanation.direct: The tactic collapses when the lure still leaves you reactive or makes your dependence too visible.
explanation.competitive: Exactly. A needy lure gives the board away again.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 8 follow from Chapter 7's concern with visible ownership?
choices: It drops the ownership issue and focuses only on private emotion
It moves earlier and asks who controls the field before any visible result exists to be owned
It argues that authorship means you should always chase first

explanation.gentle: That is the connection. Chapter 7 dealt with ownership after outcomes appear, and Chapter 8 moves back to control of contact and movement before that point.
explanation.direct: The sequence matters: before someone owns the visible result, someone often controls who approached and on what terms.
explanation.competitive: Right. Before the crown gets assigned, somebody has to build the board.

questions.prompt: If others are now stepping onto your chosen ground, what question naturally opens the next chapter?
choices: How do you make every argument longer than necessary
Why should bait replace all direct action forever
What wins more reliably once contact becomes direct: argument or visible action

explanation.gentle: Yes. The next chapter follows the moment after approach has happened and asks what actually settles the contest.
explanation.direct: Chapter 8 leads into Chapter 9 by moving from control of movement to the stronger issue of proving force through action rather than words.
explanation.competitive: That is the bridge. Once they step onto your board, the next test is whether the speech or the move carries the win.
